Title: A Survey of Distributed Denial of Service Attacks and Defenses
Text:
A Survey of Distributed Denial of Service Atacks and Defenses
RAJAT TANDON, University of Southern California, Information Sciences Institute
A distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) atack is an atack wherein multiple compromised computer systems
ﬂood the bandwidth and/or resources of a target, such as a server, website or other network resource, and
cause a denial of service for users of the targeted resource. Te ﬂood of incoming messages, connection
requests or malformed packets to the target system forces it to slow down or even crash and shut down,
thereby denying service to legitimate users or systems. Tis paper presents a literature review of DDoS atacks
and the common defense mechanisms available. It also presents a literature review of the defenses for low-rate
DDoS atacks that have not been handled eﬀectively hitherto.
1
INTRODUCTION
Although diﬀerent researches are ﬁghting against DDoS atacks, even today, the deployment or
development of eﬀective methods and mechanisms of these researches cannot resist DDoS atacks.
It is a hard problem to solve because it is multifaceted. Tere are multifarious ways of creating
atacks that are extremely eﬀective. Section 2 and 3 give an overview of the classiﬁcation and
types of the diﬀerent DDoS atacks. Section 4 gives an overview of the commonly used defense
mechanisms. I am interested in working on types of atacks that so far we have not been able to
handle eﬀectively. Tese are mainly low-rate atacks and their related works are mentioned in
Section 5.
DDoS atacks possess immense threat to the current Internet community, which comprises over
3.5 billion users [28]. Figure 1 shows the year-wise growth statistics of DDoS atacks, collated from
Arbor Networks: Worldwide Infrastructure Security Report [3], Calyptix Security Blog [8], DDoS
atack on Dyn[11] in 2016 and the largest volumetric DDoS atack, ever recorded, on Github [12].
Te 2016 Dyn cyberatack[11], that took place on October 21, 2016 included multiple DDoS atacks
targeting systems operated by Domain Name System (DNS) provider Dyn. It caused major Internet
platforms and services to be unavailable to a large number of users spread across Europe and North
America. And the magnitude of these atacks peaked to 1.2 Tbps.
Te Github DDoS atack[12] generated a ﬂood of internet traﬃc that peaked at 1.35Tbps, making
it the largest on record. Interestingly, no botnets were involved in this atack. Instead, the hackers
went with an ampliﬁcation atack. Tey spoofed GitHub’s IP address, and sent queries to several
memcached servers that are typically used to speed up database-driven sites. Te memcached
systems then sent ampliﬁed responses from those requests to GitHub.
A computer or networked device under the control of an intruder is known as a bot. In general, in
a DDoS atack, an atacker begins by exploiting a vulnerability in a computer system, making it the
DDoS master bot. Te atack master system identiﬁes other vulnerable systems and gains control
over them by either infecting the systems with malware or through bypassing the authentication
controls. Tese systems are called DDoS slave bots. Te atacker creates a command-and-control
server to command the network of bots, referred to as a botnet.[25] Ten, the atacker uses the
traﬃc generated by the compromised devices to inundate the target so as to get its services down.
Figure 2 represents a typical DDoS architecture [14].
Also, the atackers aim that the DDoS atack packets do not reveal any obvious characteristic
to segregate malicious and legitimate traﬃc. With minimal eﬀort, the atackers aim to create the
maximum-possible catastrophic impact.

Te reasons or motivations behind DDoS atacks can be speciﬁc. But, in general, the major
causes for DDoS atacks are as follows:
(1) Competition: DDoS atacks can be intended to cripple company operations, damage repu-
tation and devastate sales, which may directly beneﬁt competitors.
(2) Financial Gains: DDoS atacks can be used to achieve ﬁnancial gains. Atackers can be
hired, paid well or can even ask for ransom.
(3) Politics: DDoS atacks have the potential to digitally silence opposition parties. Tey can
be used by political parties and terrorists.
(4) Revenge: Current employees, ex-employees, angry customers or anyone with a dispute
may have a motive for a DDoS atack.

2
CLASSIFICATION OF DDOS ATTACKS
Tere are a wide variety of possible DDoS atacks. And it is challenging to represent all of them
with a single classiﬁcation. Diﬀerent literatures have classiﬁed DDoS atacks in diﬀerent ways
[17, 27, 34, 43]. Arbor networks have classiﬁed DDoS atacks as volumetric atacks and application
layer atacks. Volumetric atacks send a huge amount of traﬃc, or request packets, to a targeted
network so as to overwhelm its bandwidth capabilities. Typically request sizes are in the 100’s
of Gbps. However, recent atacks have scaled to over 1Tbps. Application-layer atacks generally
require a lot less packets and bandwidth to get a website down. Tey are silent and small, when
compared to network-layer atacks, but extremely disruptive.
Reference [27] presents the taxonomy of DDoS atacks and the diﬀerent classiﬁcations include
degree of automation, exploited weaknesses to deny service, source address validity, atack rate
dynamics, possibility of characterization, persistence of agent set, victim type and impact on victim.
Reference [34] portrays a taxonomy of a few major DDoS atacks, shown in Figure 3. It includes
two major classes of DDoS atacks: bandwidth depletion and resource depletion atacks. Bandwidth
depletion atacks ﬂood the victim network with undesired traﬃc, preventing legitimate traﬃc from
reaching the victim. And resource depletion atacks tie up the resources of a victim system making
the victim unable to process legitimate requests.
3
DIFFERENT DDOS ATTACKS
Te diﬀerent DDoS atacks are enumerated below:
3.1
Volumetric DDoS Atacks
Te volumetric DDoS atacks generate huge volumes of atack request or response traﬃc, usually
measured in Gigabits per second (Gbps). Te concept of a volumetric atack is simple, which is
3


to send as much traﬃc as possible to a site to overwhelm its bandwidth. Some of the well known
volumetric DDoS atacks are as follows:
(1) DNS Ampliﬁcation Atack: A DNS ampliﬁcation atack is a DDoS atack in which the
atacker exploits vulnerabilities in domain name system (DNS) servers to turn initially
small queries into much larger payloads, which are used to bring down the victimﬁs servers.
It is a reﬂection atack that manipulates publicly-accessible domain name systems, making
them ﬂood a target with large quantities of UDP packets. Using various ampliﬁcation
techniques, perpetrators can ﬁinﬂateﬁthe size of these UDP packets, making the atack so
potent as to bring down even the most robust Internet infrastructure.
(2) CharGEN Ampliﬁcation Atack: A CharGEN ampliﬁcation atack is usually carried out by
sending small packets carrying a spoofed IP address of the target to the internet enabled
devices running CharGEN. Tese spoofed requests to such devices are then used to send
UDP ﬂoods as responses from these devices to the target. Internet-enabled printers and
copiers have this protocol enabled by default and can be used to execute a CharGEN
atack. Tis can be used to ﬂood a target with UDP packets on port number 19. Te server
eventually exhausts its resources and goes down.
(3) SNMP Ampliﬁcation Atack: Simple Network Management Protocol(SNMP) is used for
network management. SNMP ampliﬁcation atack is carried out by sending small packets
carrying spoofed IP address of the target to the internet enabled devices running SNMP.
Tese spoofed requests to such devices are then used to send UDP ﬂoods as responses from
these devices to the target. However, ampliﬁcation eﬀect in SNMP can be greater when
compared with CHARGEN and DNS atacks. When the target tries to make sense of this
ﬂood of requests, it will end up exhausting its resources and will go down.
(4) NTP Ampliﬁcation Atack: Network Time Protocol(NTP) is used to synchronize the clocks
of computers to some time reference. Te NTP protocol is another publicly accessible
network protocol. NTP ampliﬁcation is essentially a reﬂection atack. Reﬂection atacks
involve eliciting a response from a server to a spoofed IP address. Te atacker sends a
packet with a forged IP address, which belongs to the victim and the server replies to this
address. Te response is considerably larger than the request, amplifying the amount of
traﬃc directed at the target server and ultimately leading to a degradation of service for
legitimate requests.
(5) SSDP Ampliﬁcation Atack: Te Simple Service Discovery Protocol(SSDP) is based on the
Internet Protocol Suite for advertisement and discovery of network services and presence
information. SSDP allows universal plug and play devices to send and receive information
using UDP on port number 1900. SSDP is atractive to DDoS atackers because of its open
state that allows spooﬁng and ampliﬁcation. Te atacker conducts a scan looking for
plug-and-play devices that can be utilized as ampliﬁcation factors. As the atacker discovers
networked devices, they create a list of all the devices that respond. Te atacker creates a
UDP packet with the spoofed IP address of the targeted victim. Te atacker then uses a
botnet to send a spoofed discovery packet to each plug-and-play device with a request for
as much data as possible by seting certain ﬂags, speciﬁcally ssdp:rootdevice or ssdp:all. As
a result, each device will send a reply to the targeted victim with huge response. Te target
then receives a large volume of traﬃc from all the devices and becomes overwhelmed and
results in denial-of-service to legitimate traﬃc.
(6) UDP Flood Atack: User Datagram Protocol(UDP) is a connectionless protocol that uses
datagrams embedded in IP packets for communication without creating a session between
two devices. In a UDP Flood atack, a lot of UDP packets are sent to either random or
4


speciﬁc ports on the victim system. In order to determine the requested application, the
victim system processes the incoming data. In case of absence of the requested application
on the requested port, the victim system sends a ”Destination unreachable” message to the
sender. Also, to conceal the identity, the atacker ofen spoofs the source IP address of the
atacking packets. UDP ﬂood atacks ofen deplete the bandwidth of network around the
victim’s system. Tereby, the systems close to the victim are also impacted due to the UDP
ﬂooding atack.
3.2
Protocol Atacks
An internet protocol is basically a discrete set of rules to exchange information on the internet.
Tese rules can be exploited by a bad actor. Some of the well known protocol atacks are as follows:
(1) TCP SYN Flood Atack: Te Transmission Control Protocol(TCP) SYN Flood atack is a
DDoS atack that exploits the design of the three way TCP communication process between
a client, host, and server. First, a client initiates a new session by sending a SYN packet
to the server. Te server responds with a SYNACK packet and then the client sends an
ACK packet to the server before a connection is established. In a SYN ﬂood atack, the
atacker sends repeated SYN packets to every port on the targeted server, ofen using fake
IP addresses. Te server, unaware of the atack, receives multiple, apparently legitimate
looking requests to establish communication. It responds to each of these with a SYN-ACK
packet from each open port. Before the connection can time out, another SYN packet
arrives. Tis leaves an increasingly large number of half-open connections. Ultimately, the
serverﬁs connection overﬂow tables get ﬂooded and the service to legitimate clients are
denied. Finally, the server may even malfunction or crash.
(2) TCP SYN-ACK Flood Atack: Te second step of the three-way TCP communication process
is exploited by this DDoS atack. In a TCP SYN-ACK DDoS atack, atackers send spoofed
SYN packets to a large numbers of servers and proxies on the Internet that generate large
numbers of SYN-ACK packets in response to incoming SYN requests from the spoofed
atackers. Tis SYN-ACK ﬂood is not directed back to the botnet, but instead, is directed
back to victimﬁs network and ofen exhausts the victimﬁs ﬁrewalls by forcing state-table
lookups for every incoming SYN-ACK packet. Tis denial of service atack can render
stateful devices inoperable and can also consume excessive amounts of resources on routers,
servers and IPS/IDS devices.
(3) PUSH+ACK Flood Atack: When connecting with a server, the client can ask for conﬁrma-
tion that the information was received by seting the ACK ﬂag, or it can force the server
to process the information in the packet by seting the PUSH ﬂag. Both requests require
the server to do more work than with other types of requests. By ﬂooding a server with
spurious PUSH and ACK requests, an atacker can prevent the server from responding to
valid traﬃc.
(4) RST/FIN Flood Atack: Afer a successful three or four-way TCP-SYN session, RST or FIN
packets are exchanged by servers to close the TCP-SYN session between a host and a client
machine. In an RST or FIN Flood atack, a target server receives a large number of spoofed
RST or FIN packets that do not belong to any session on the target server. Tis atack tries
to exhaust a serverﬁs resources as the server tries to process these invalid requests. Te
result is a server unavailable to process legitimate requests due to resources exhaustion.
(5) IGMP Flood Atack: Internet Group Management Protocol(IGMP) is yet another connec-
tionless protocol, used by IP hosts to report or leave their multicast group memberships for
adjacent routers. An IGMP ﬂood atack involves a large number of IGMP message reports
5


being sent to a network or router, signiﬁcantly slowing down and eventually preventing
legitimate traﬃc from being transmited across the target network.
(6) ICMP Flood Atack/Ping Flood Atack: Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) is another
connectionless protocol used for IP operations, diagnostics, and errors. Just as with a UDP
ﬂood, an ICMP ﬂood does not rely on any speciﬁc vulnerability to achieve denial-of-service.
An ICMP ﬂood atack can involve an ICMP echo request. Once enough ICMP traﬃc is sent
to a target server, it gets overwhelmed with requests, resulting in a denial-of-service.
(7) Multi-Vector Atack: Atackers can also combine more than one DDoS atack mechanisms
to ﬁre DDoS atacks keeping the engineers dealing with the DDoS atack confused. Tese
atacks are the hard to discern and are capable of taking down some of the best-protected
servers and networks. For example, HTTP Flood Atack can be combined with Recursive
HTTP GET Flood Atack and ﬁred together.
(8) DNS Flood Atack: In a Domain Name System(DNS) ﬂood atack, the atacker targets one or
more DNS servers belonging to a given zone, atempting to hamper resolution of resource
records of that zone and its sub-zones. DNS servers help requesters ﬁnd the servers they
seek. A DNS zone is a distinct portion of the domain name space in the Domain Name
System. Te administrative responsibility is delegated to a single server cluster for each
zone. In a DNS ﬂood atack the oﬀender tries to overbear DNS servers with apparently valid
traﬃc, overwhelming server resources and impeding the servers’ ability to direct legitimate
requests to zone resources. Te atacker sends multiple DNS requests to the victimﬁs DNS
server directly or via a botnet. Te DNS servers become ﬂooded with requests,cannot
process all of its incoming requests, eventually crashes.
(9) Smurf Atack: Te Smurf atack is a DDoS atack in which a large number of ICMP packets
with the intended victim’s spoofed source IP are broadcast to a computer network using an
IP broadcast address. Most devices on a network will, by default, respond to this by sending
a reply to the source IP address. If the number of machines on the network that receive and
respond to these packets is very large, the victim’s computer will be ﬂooded with traﬃc.
Tis can slow down the victim’s computer to the point where it becomes impossible to
work on.
(10) Fraggle Atack: A Fraggle Atack is a DDoS atack that involves sending a large amount of
spoofed UDP traﬃc to a routerﬁs broadcast address within a network. It is very similar to
a Smurf Atack.
(11) SIP Flood Atack: Te Session Initiation Protocol(SIP) ﬂood atack is a DDoS atack that
exploits the application layer protocol SIP, used in VOIP call setup. An atack can be made
using diﬀerent types of SIP request messages like SIP REQUEST, SIP INVITE or the SIP call
control messages like SIP INFO, SIP NOTIFY, SIP RE-INVITE. Te goal of this atack is to
ﬂood the proxy server or the SIP registration server and to consume all of its resources.
Here, any army from the botnet sends thousands of messages to the SIP registrar server
which is responsible to accept REGISTRAR requests as well as to keep records of the
addresses and parameters of the user agents, unless it receives any server error message. As
a result, the server overwhelms the legitimate users experience service outage and cannot
reach the server.
(12) IP Null Atack: Packets contain IPv4 headers which carry information about which transport
protocol is being used. When atackers set the value of this ﬁeld to zero, these packets can
bypass security measures designed to scan TCP, IP, and ICMP. When the target server tries
to put process these packets, it will eventually exhaust its resources and reboot.
6


(13) HTTP Flood Atack: Te real IP of the bots is used to avoid suspicion. Te number of
bots used to execute the atack is same as the source IP range for this atack. Since the IP
addresses of the bots are not spoofed, there is no reason for defense mechanisms to ﬂag
these valid HTTP requests. A bot can be used to send a large number of GET, POST or
other HTTP requests to execute an atack. Many bots can be collated in an HTTP DDoS
atack to completely cripple the target server.
(14) Single Session HTTP Flood: An atacker can exploit a loophole in HTTP 1.1 to send several
requests from a single HTTP session. Tis allows atackers to send a large number of
requests from a handful of sessions. In other words, atackers can bypass the limitations
imposed by DDoS defense mechanisms on the number of sessions allowed. Single Session
HTTP ﬂood atacks target a serverﬁs resources resulting in complete system shutdown or
poor performance of the server.
(15) Single Request HTTP Flood Atack: Single request HTTP Flood atack is based on the idea
of sending several HTTP requests in a single HTTP session by masking these requests
within one HTTP packet. When defense mechanisms evolved to block multiple incoming
packets for a single session, atacks like Single Packet HTTP Flood were designed with
workarounds to defeat these defenses. Tis evolution of an HTTP ﬂood exploits another
loophole in the HTTP technology. Several HTTP requests can be made by a single HTTP
session by masking these requests within one HTTP packet. Keeping packet rates within
the allowed limits, this technique allows an eﬀective atack, exhausting a serverﬁs resources.
(16) Recursive HTTP GET Flood Atack: For an atack to be highly successful, it must remain
undetected for as long as possible. Tis is yet another kind of HTTP ﬂood atack wherein
the atacker requests multiple website pages, analyses replies, and then recursively requests
each object of the website. Tis method can be used together with any kind of HTTP to
make the atack as unnoticeable as possible. It is hard to detect as the recursive requests of
the website objects resemble legitimate requests.
(17) Random Recursive GET Flood Atack: Tis atack is a purpose built variation of Recursive
GET atack. It is designed for forums, blogs and other websites that have pages in a sequence.
Like Recursive GET it also appears to be going through pages. Since page names are in
a sequence, to keep up appearance as a legitimate user, it uses random numbers from
a valid page range to send a new GET request each time. Random Recursive GET also
aims to deﬂate its targetﬁs performance with a large number of GET requests leading to
denial-of-service for actual legitimate users.
(18) IP Packet Option Field Atack: Tis atack targets the optional ﬁelds of an IP packet and
randomizes its value. For example, if in an IP packet, all qualities of service bits are set
to 1, it causes the victim to apply some additional time to analyze the packet. Tus, it
can inundate the processing ability of the victim if a ﬂood of packets arrives with such
deformation.
(19) Ping of Death Atack: In a ping of death atack, an atacker intentionally forms a data packet
that exceeds the maximum packet size which causes the victims to freeze or crash. Tis
atack can be initiated by the atacker without requiring a botnet. It is an IP fragmentation
atack that exploits the inherent size limitation that a packet can be transmited in.
(20) Teardrop Atack: In this atack, the atacker manipulates the oﬀset value which in turn
generates errors in fragmentation and reassembly of packets. Te atacker sends fragmented
packets with overlapping oﬀset numbers. Tus, during the time of the packet re-assembly,
invalid packets are created and crash the targeted server.
7


(21) Session Atack: To bypass defenses, instead of using spoofed IP addresses, this atack uses
the real IP address of the bots being used to carry out an atack. Tis atack is executed
by creating a TCP-SYN session between a bot and the target server. Tis session is then
stretched out until it times out by delaying the ACK packets. Session atacks try to exhaust
a server’s resources through these empty sessions. Tat, in turn, results in a complete
system shutdown or unacceptable system performance.
(22) UDP Fragmentation Flood Atack: It is another one of those cleverly masked DDoS atacks
that are not easily detected. Te activity generated by this atack resembles valid traﬃc
and all of it is kept within limits. Tis version of the UDP Flood atack sends larger
yet fragmented packets to exhaust more bandwidth by sending fewer fragmented UDP
packets.When a target server tries to put these unrelated and forged fragmented UDP
packets together, it will fail to do so. Eventually, all available resources are exhausted and
the server goes down.
(23) VoIP Flood Atack: Tis version of application speciﬁc UDP ﬂood atack targets VoIP servers.
An atacker sends a large number of spoofed VoIP request packets from a very large set of
source IP. When a VoIP server is ﬂooded with spoofed requests, it exhausts all available
resources while trying to serve the valid and invalid requests.
Tis reboots the server or takes a toll on the serverﬁs performance and exhausts the
available bandwidth. VoIP ﬂoods can contain ﬁxed or random source IP. Fixed source IP
address atack is not easy to detect as it masks itself and looks no diﬀerent from legitimate
traﬃc.
(24) ICMP Fragmentation Flood Atack: Tis version of ICMP Flood atack sends larger packets
to exhaust more bandwidth by sending fewer fragmented ICMP packets. When the target
server tries to put these forged fragmented ICMP packets with no correlation together, it
will fail to do so. Te server eventually exhausts its resources and reboots.
3.3
Low Rate DDoS Atacks
Detection of low rate DDoS atacks is extremely hard as they possess the ability of concealing their
traﬃc, because the traﬃc is very much like the normal, legitimate traﬃc. Tey are able to elude the
current anomaly-based detection schemes. Some of the well known low rate DDoS atacks are as
follows:
(1) Flash-Crowd DDoS Atacks: A Flash Crowd Atack(FCA) is a DDoS atack that consumes
the resources of a targeted service with legitimate looking requests generated by numerous
bots. It is extremely hard to detect as bots may request legitimate content. An atacker may
further employ several bots, each sending requests at a low rate.
(2) TCP Shrew Atack: Tese are DDoS atacks which generate periodic, short bursts of high-
volume traﬃc and create congestion. Tis forces legitimate TCP connections to drastically
reduce their sending rate. Shrew atacks exploit, the deﬁciencies in the retransmission
time-out (RTO) mechanism of TCP ﬂows. Tey throtle legitimate TCP ﬂows by periodically
sending burst pulses with high peak rate in a low frequency. As such, the TCP ﬂows see
congestion on the atacked link every time it recovers from RTO. Indeed, such a shrew
atack may reduce the throughput of TCP applications down to almost zero.
(3) Hash Collisions DDoS Atacks: Most application servers create hash tables to index POST
session parameters and are sometimes required to manage hash collisions when similar
hash values are returned. Collision resolutions are resource intensive, as they require an
additional amount of CPU to process the requests. In Hash Collision DDoS atacks, the
atacker sends a specially crafed POST message with a multitude of parameters. Tese
8


parameters are built in a way that causes hash collisions on the server side. Tis slows
down the response processing dramatically. Hash Collisions DDoS atacks are very eﬀective
and can be launched from a single atacker computer, slowly exhausting the application
serverﬁs resources.
(4) Costly Requests Atack: Tese are DDoS atacks wherein the atacker requests for content
that requires costly database queries, which deplete bandwidth and connection pool between
a front-end server and a database. Te requests that involve long processing times, create a
load on database processing and consume ample amount of server resources are selected
by the atackers to launch the atack.
(5) Slowloris Atack: A Slowloris DDoS atack works by opening multiple connections to
the targeted web server. And it keeps them open as long as possible. Tis is achieved
by continuously sending partial HTTP requests, none of which are ever completed. Te
atacked servers open more and connections open, waiting for each of the atack requests
to be completed. As the requests are not completed, the targeted serverﬁs maximum
concurrent connection pool gets ﬁlled, and additional legitimate connection atempts are
denied.
3.4
Vulnerability-Based DDoS Atacks
Servers or protocols may have are unknown or unpatched vulnerabilities. Atackers exploit these
vulnerabilities to launch atacks. Examples of vulnerability-based DDoS atacks are:
(1) Zero Day DDoS Atack: Tese are DDoS atacks that exploit new vulnerabilities. Tese
ZERO Day DDoS vulnerabilities do not have patches or eﬀective defensive mechanisms at
the time of the atack.
(2) LAND Atack: A LAND(Local Area Network Denial) atack is a DDoS atack that consists
of sending a special poison spoofed packets to a computer, causing it to lock up. Whenever
a system receives this type of packets, it replies back to itself which in turn creates an
inﬁnite loop. As a result of this, the system crashes eventually.
4
DDOS MITIGATION
DDoS atacks pose immense threat to the resources of the victim and to the network bandwidth
and infrastructure. Although for each atack, or a group of atacks, described in Section 3, there are
speciﬁc defense mechanisms available in literature, some of the commonly used ways to mitigate
DDoS atacks are as follows:
(1) Hop-count ﬁltering: A commonly used defense is hop-count ﬁltering [19] that ﬁlters packets
that contain spoofed IP addresses. In this approach, the authors have used the concept
that it is not possible to alter the number of hops of an IP packet when it travels from
a source to a destination. Terefore, the authors have used this count to determine the
validity of a packet. In this method, time to live value is used to count the number of hops.
Tis hop counts are stored in a mapping table against each source address. Upon receiving
a packet, the number of hops required for this packet is calculated and matched against
the mapping table. A packet is detected as spoofed packet if a mismatch is found in this
comparison. If a ﬂow of packets is identiﬁed as a ﬂow of spoofed packets, the ﬁlter discards
those packets as a prevention of an atack. Te deployment of such a technique is easier as
it requires implementation in the victim’s system. But, it has a limitation in the process of
hop count. As this method counts the number of hops based on time to live, the number
of false positive is larger in this method. Tis is because the initial time to live value is
usually diﬀerent for diﬀerent operating systems. Additionally, the atacker can forge valid
9


hop counts in their packets which allows the packets to pass the ﬁlter. Finally, for a ﬂood
of malicious packets, the system cannot perform the calculation and comparison. Hence it
becomes the victim of the DDoS atack.
(2) Source Address Validity Enforcement protocol: Source Address Validity Enforcement (SAVE)
protocol [24] enforces the routers to send messages containing updated source information
to each destination routers connected to a source. Ten, each router updates its forwarding
table with current information and uses it to ﬁlter the packets based on the methods of RPF.
Tus, it overcomes the problem encountered in the RPF for the asymmetric and dynamic
nature of the Internet. However, implementation of such protocol requires a change in the
existing routing protocol which is a time-consuming process. Also, a partial deployment of
the protocol does not guarantee full success in ﬁltering spoofed IP addresses.
(3) Rate Limiting: Rate limiting is one of common ways to defend the DDoS atacks. Generally,
if the results of a detection mechanism are found to be partially successful, that is, if it
produces large false negatives or cannot identify a precise distinction between the legitimate
and malicious traﬃc, it is reasonable to apply rate limiting rather than ﬁltering.
(4) Ingress/Egress ﬁltering: Ingress/Egress ﬁltering is a commonly used technique to prevent
traﬃc with spoofed IP addresses to enter into a protected network. Basically, ingress
ﬁltering ﬁlters the malicious traﬃc destined to a local network and egress ﬁltering discards
the malicious traﬃc leaving a local network. Ingress ﬁltering deﬁned in RFC 226768 allows
the traﬃc to enter the network which matches with a predeﬁned range of domain preﬁxes
of the network. If an atacker uses spoofed IP address that do not match with the preﬁxes,
it is discarded at the routers. Tus, this ﬁltering technique ensures prevention from DDoS
atacks where spoofed IP addresses are used. However, it is not a useful mechanism in the
cases where the valid IP addresses of the botnets are used as a source IP addresses during
the atack. Also, the success of these ﬁltering depends on the knowledge of the range
of expected IP addresses for a port which is not always achievable for the complicated
topologies used in diﬀerent networks. Moreover, if an atacker uses some spoofed IP
addresses that fall into the valid address range, the ﬁlters in the routers cannot detect the
malicious traﬃc in such scenarios. Also, for these ﬁlters, itunneling is required for mobile
IP users so that they are not ﬁltered by the routers using ingress/egress ﬁltering. Moreover,
as it does not ensure incentives to the Internet Service Providers, it is partially deployed in
the networks. Additionally, many Internet Service Providers do not enforce this approach.
(5) Load balancing: Te key function of a load balancer is to spread workloads across multiple
servers to prevent overloading servers, optimize productivity, and maximize uptime. Load
balancers also add resiliency by re-routing live traﬃc from one server to another if a
server is under a DDoS atack. Terefore, load balancers help to eliminate single points
of failure and reduce the atack surface. Load Balancing is an approach which tries to
balance the loads of diﬀerent systems so that no one system gets overloaded. Te result
of the load balancing helps to gain the optimal productivity and the maximum uptime.
In order to ensure the maximum load balancing, a bandwidth increase is required on all
critical connections. A good number of replicated servers and data centers are required to
guarantee elimination of single point of failure.
(6) Martian address ﬁltering and source address validation: Martian address ﬁltering is deﬁned
in RFC 1812. It works for ﬁltering spoofed IP addresses that are generated from a limited set
of addresses. Tis ﬁltering ensures that a router must not forward any packet which has an
invalid source or destination IP address. Tese invalid IP addresses range from reserved or
special IP addresses as well as the unallocated range of IP addresses. Additionally, it ensures
10


that any packet with the destination IP address 255.255.255.255/32 must be discarded at the
router.
Source address validation is also speciﬁed in RFC 1812 and implemented in the routers.
In this ﬁltering mechanism, the router compares the source address of a packet with the
logical interface of the packet where it is received. If this interface does not match with
the interface where the packet needs to be destined to reach the speciﬁed source address,
the router discards the packet. Tus, it can ﬁlter packets with spoofed source IP addresses.
However, the rate of the false positive may become high for the asymmetric routes of the
Internet. Tis asymmetric nature does not guarantee the match of the interfaces upon
receiving or return of a packet from a speciﬁc source address. Tus, this ﬁltering may
discard a large number of legitimate traﬃcs. However, the essential issue here is that not
all routers in the Internet implement these approaches.
(7) Capability-based response: Tis mechanism can help prevent ﬂooding related DDoS atacks.
Te receiver cannot control how much traﬃc it would receive. Tere exists ﬂow control and
congestion control mechanisms, but a misbehaving sender does not care about it. Terefore,
the techniques involved in capability-based DDoS response work to discern a solution to
control such misbehaving sender. Stateless inter ﬂow ﬁlter (SIFF)134 and traﬃc validation
architecture (TVA)135 are two example methods of this type.
(8) Route-based Packet Filtering: Route-based Packet Filtering(RPF) ﬁlters packets with spoofed
source IP addresses. Tis ﬁltering technique enhances the scope of the ingress ﬁltering by
providing service to the core routers. It does provide ﬁltering based on the route information
of a packet in each link of a core router. It depends on the principle that each link of the
core router accepts traﬃc from only a limited number of source addresses. Tus, an IP
packet which has a diﬀerent source address than this set of addresses is discarded by the
core routers as it appears to be spoofed to the router. In order to implement this technique,
it requires information of the Border Gateway Protocol routing topology. According to the
simulation of Park and Lee,[29] a signiﬁcant success of the technique will be achieved if
18% of the autonomous systems implement this ﬁltering technique. However, this number
is found impractical in current Internet scenario. Additionally, in order to include the
source addresses in the BGP message, it is required to modify the scheme used in BGP
messaging. Tis increases the message size and processing time of the BGP messages.
Moreover, if the routers do not maintain updated information, this technique can discard
legitimate packets for unwanted root change. Also, as RPF ﬁlters packets are based on
BGP messaging information, an atacker can deceive root information and ﬁltering rules
by stealing BGP sessions. Finally, the atacker can carefully choose IP addresses that do
not resemble the spoofed IPs. Tis can make the method ineﬀective in protecting DDoS
from spoofed IP. Reference [15] extends the idea of Park and Lee[29] by designing a packet
ﬁltering mechanism which considers update messages of local BGP to ﬁlter out spoofed IP
addresses. Tis method is easy to deploy on the current architecture which relies on the
BGP routing protocol. It also reduces the rate of false positive and simpliﬁes IP traceback
process.
(9) History-based ﬁltering: History-based ﬁltering is a packet markingﬁ?based ﬁltering tech-
nique where the history of the normal traﬃc is used to ﬁlter out the malicious traﬃc[30].
Here, the destination of an atack maintains a database of IP addresses. Tis database
comprises IP addresses which are commonly found in the destination. Terefore, when a
bandwidth atack is targeted to this system, the system only allows those IP addresses that
appear in their database and discards all other IP packets. However, this ﬁltering technique
11


cannot successfully detect and discard the malicious ﬂow if an atacker can simulate its
atack traﬃc as a normal traﬃc.
(10) Path identiﬁer: Te path identiﬁer method [39] eliminates packets based on a path identiﬁer
that identiﬁes the path of the atacker. Identifying the path is a deterministic approach
where each packet is stamped with an identiﬁer based on the path it has traveled. Te
packets that travel the same path contain the same identiﬁer. Tus, if the victim can
identify a packet traveling from the atacker, it can ﬁlter all the subsequent packets sent
by the atacker. Tis approach works well when half of the routers get involved to mark
the packets. Because it works with a small sized identiﬁcation ﬁeld, there remains the
possibility that diﬀerent paths can show the same path information. Terefore, it can give
false-positives and false-negatives. Reference [40] proposes an improved version of the
path identiﬁer approach called StackPi that improves path identiﬁer’s performance in terms
of incremental deployment. Additionally the improved ﬁltering mechanism is capable of
identifying malicious ﬂows based on just a single packet. As per the paper, this method
can provide a reasonable amount of DDoS protection only if 20% of the routers implement
this marking scheme. However, this method does not consider the detection of spoofed IP
address packets rather it marks and ﬁlters a malicious packet based on the deterministic
packet marking mechanism. Moreover, a host or router looking for the path information
through this method may need to have some supportive sofware as well as expense of
processing making this method diﬃcult to deploy, as mentioned in reference [4].
(11) PacketScore: PacketScore [21] is a proactive ﬁltering technique that uses Bayes theorem to
compute conditional legitimate probability(CLP). Te conditional legitimate probability
is used to determine the likelihood of a legitimate packet based on the baseline proﬁle
value and the atribute value of a packet. Te packet ﬁltering works based on this CLP
value and a dynamic threshold. As the ﬁltering takes into account the statistical analysis,
this method works well for new atack signatures as well as non spoofed atack traﬃcs.
However, this method requires a large amount of storage to deal with the increasing
number of atack atributes. It introduces a DDoS defense scheme that supports automated
online atack characterizations and accurate atack packet discarding based on statistical
processing. Te key idea is to prioritize a packet based on a score which estimates its
legitimacy given the atribute values it carries. Once the score of a packet is computed, this
scheme performs score-based selective packet discarding where the dropping threshold is
dynamically adjusted based on the score distribution of recent incoming packets and the
current level of system overload.
(12) Secure overlay: Te idea behind secure overlay [1] is to build up an overlay network on top
of the IP network. It uses three principles: (i) enabling end-hosts to communicate without
revealing their IP address, (ii) giving end-hosts control to defend against Denial-of-Service
(DoS) atacks at the overlay level, and (iii) making sure that the added functionality does
not introduce vulnerabilities not present in the Internet. Tis overlay network is the entry
point for the outside network to establish a communication to the protected network. It is
assumed that the isolation can be achieved if a protected network hides its IP addresses or
uses a distributed ﬁrewall. Tis ﬁrewall ensures that only trusted traﬃc from the nodes
of the overlay network can get entry to the protected network. Although this mechanism
ensures prevention from the DDoS atack, it is applicable to a private network.
(13) Honeypots: A honeypot [35] atracts atackers to atack them. Terefore, the actual sys-
tem remains protected. Also, honeypots can be used to extract important information
like records of atack activity, tools, and sofware used for the atack which can reveal
12


information about an atacker. Tis information is further used to detect and mitigate a
DDoS atack. But this technique also contains some drawbacks. For example, the static and
passive nature of the honeypots do not guarantee complete concealing from the atacker.
(14) Changing IP addresses: Changing IP address technique [16] allows the computer system
changes its IP address to invalidate an old address which may be the potential target of
the DDoS atacks. Tis approach works for an IP address based atack. However, this
also incurs a lot of overheads such as updating diﬀerent entry information. Tis method
works well till the atacker does not get informed about the new IP address. Tis approach
provides the technological futility of addressing the problem solely at the local level.
(15) Congestion policing: Te goal of a bandwidth ﬂooding atack is to congest the resource[13].
Te impact of this type of atacks can be reduced or eliminated by applying congestion
policing mechanism. Re-feedback[6] and NetFence[26] are two example mechanisms where
congestion policing is applied to defend DDoS atacks. Re-feedback ensures metrics in data
headers such as time to live and congestion notiﬁcation will arrive at each relay carrying
a truthful prediction of the remainder of their path. NetFence uses a secure congestion
policing feedback, to enable robust congestion policing inside the network.
(16) Applying security patches: It is also required to update all security patches regularly to
ensure that the system is not aﬀected by bugs or worms. Also, in order to prevent IoT
botnetﬁs generation, it is mandatory to change the default or generic passwords of the IoT
devices.86 Tis is an important awareness from the users side that can ﬁght against the
massive IoTﬁ?based DDoS atacks. However, the irony is that most of the users of the
IoT devices are not aware of the threats or even they do not know the name of the DDoS
atacks. When an atacker compromises a device for the DDoS army, the user of the device
does not notice any change in their performance or behavior. Tus, stealthily they help in
the atack without even knowing the name of the atack that they are participating.
5
DEFENSES FOR LOW RATE ATTACKS
Low-rate DDoS atacks are not handled eﬀectively by the current defense mechanisms. Tese
atacks have ability of concealing their traﬃc because they are very much like normal traﬃc. Tey
have the capacity to elude the current anomaly-based detection schemes. Instead of exhausting the
network bandwidth, these atacks deny service at the device level. Tey deplete the resources at
the service or the operating system, making it diﬃcult for the device unable to process legitimate
clients’ traﬃc. Tese atacks are challenging to detect at the network level since they generate
requests at low rate. Examples of such atacks are Flash Crowd Atack, TCP Shrew Atack[22],
Slowloris Atack, Hash-Collision Atack, described in 3.3.
Instead of a generic approach, most defenses focus on just a single variant. Tere is no generic
framework to handle all low-rate DDoS atacks.
Some related work for the slow atacks is as follows:
(1) Reference Architecture: Reference [33] proposes a reference architecture for defense against
low-rate DDoS atacks, enabled by a Sofware Deﬁned Infrastructure(SDI). Here, both
network and computational resources are provisioned and modiﬁed on demand to achieve
the mitigation goals. Te suspicious traﬃc is detected and redirected to the Shark Tank
system, which is created on-demand. Te Shark Tank system is a separate cluster which
possesses full application capabilities designed to monitor suspicious users. Te key feature
of the Shark Tank is to act as a restricted area for the atacker so that they can be placed
under close surveillance. It does absorb the damage from the DDoS atacks and allows the
system to learn from these atacks for future reference.
13


(2) Collaborative Detection and Filtering: Reference [10] presents a defense by combining
discrete Fourier transform (DFT) and a hypothesis test framework to cope with shrew
atacks. By computing the autocorrelation sequence of sampled time series and converting
them into frequency-domain spectrum using DFT, the authors ﬁnd that the power spectrum
density (PSD) of a traﬃc stream containing shrew atacks that has much higher energy
in low-frequency band than that appears in the spectrum for legitimate TCP/UDP traﬃc
streams. Based on this distinction, we develop a distributed collaborative detection and
ﬁltering (CDF) scheme to detect and segregate the shrew atack ﬂows from legitimate
TCP/UDP traﬃc ﬂows. In addition to sofware implementation, the scheme can be im-
plemented by network processor or reconﬁgurable hardware. Te DSP hardware pushes
spectral analysis down to the lower packet-processing layer. If the packets are processed by
hardware and malicious ﬂows are ﬁltered out timely, the router workload will not increase
much in the presence of shrew atacks.
(3) Randomization on TCP Retransmission Timeout (RTO): Reference [41] proposes random-
ization on TCP RTO as defense against such atacks. With RTO randomization, an atacker
cannot predict the next TCP timeout and consequently cannot inject the burst at the exact
instant. Te authors show that randomization can eﬀectively mitigate the impact of DDoS
atacks while maintaining fairness and friendliness to other connections.
(4) HAWK: Reference [23] proposes a new stateful adaptive queue management technique
called HAWK (Halting Anomaly with Weighted choKing) which works by judiciously
identifying malicious shrew packet ﬂows using a small ﬂow table and dropping such
packets decisively to halt the atack such that well-behaved TCP sessions can re-gain their
bandwidth shares. Te authors show that HAWK is highly agile.
(5) Shrew Atack Protection: Reference [9] presents a simple priority-tagging ﬁltering mecha-
nism, called SAP (Shrew Atack Protection), that protects well-behaved TCP ﬂows against
low-rate TCP-targeted Shrew atacks. In this method, a router maintains a simple set
of counters and keeps track of the drop rate for each potential victim. If the monitored
drop rates are low, all packets are treated as normal and equally compete to be admited
to the output queue and only dropped based on the AQM (Active Qeue Management)
policy when the output queue is almost full. However, if the drop rate for a certain victim
becomes higher than some dynamically determined threshold (called fair drop rate), the
router treats packets for this victim as high-priority, and these high-priority packets are
preferentially admited to the output queue. SAP marks victim packets as high priority
until their drop rate is below the fair drop rate. By preferentially dropping normal packets
to protect high-priority packets, SAP can prevent low rate TCP-targeted Shrew atacks
from causing a well-behaved TCP ﬂow to lose multiple consecutive packets repeatedly.
Tis technique protects well-behaved TCP ﬂows away from near zero throughput when
under an atack.
(6) Treat as application-level atacks and discern anomalies: A way of detecting low rate DDoS
atacks is to treat them as application-level atacks and look for anomalies in the payload
of the incoming service requests. Tis is the approach taken by DDoS defense providers
and requires costly deep-packet inspection. Reference [20] presents an investigation in
the adoption of cloud-based DDoS Protection Service providers worldwide. Te authors
focus on nine leading providers according to namely Akamai, CenturyLink, CloudFlare,
DOSarrest, F5 Networks, Incapsula, Level 3, Neustar, and Verisign. Te investigation is
done on the basis of long-term, active DNS measurements, which allows for a given domain
name, to verify if traﬃc diversion towards a DDoS Protection Service is in place or not.
14


(7) Feature Feature Score(FFSc): Reference [18] introduces a statistical measure called Feature
Feature Score (FFSc) for multivariate data analysis to distinguish DDoS atack traﬃc from
normal traﬃc. Te authors extract three features of network traﬃc, entropy of source IPs,
variation of source IPs and packet rate to analyze the behavior of network traﬃc for atack
detection. Tey build proﬁles of these features during normal operation and detect atack
traﬃc as the traﬃc that deviates from these proﬁles.
(8) New Information Metrics: Reference [37] proposes that the generalized entropy and infor-
mation distance metrics outperform the traditional Shannon entropy and Kullbackﬁ?Leibler
distance metrics for the low-rate DDoS atack detection in terms of early detection, lower
false positive rates, and stabilities. It proposes an eﬀective IP traceback scheme based on an
information distance metric that can trace all atacks back to their own local area networks
(LANs) in a short time. Te proposed generalized entropy metric can detect atacks several
hops earlier than the traditional Shannon metric approach. Te proposed information
distance metric outperforms the popular Kullback-Leibler divergence approach as it can
enlarge the adjudication distance and then obtain the optimal detection sensitivity.
(9) Expectation of Packet Size(EPS): Reference [44] presents a measurement, expectation of
packet size, that is based on the distribution diﬀerence of the packet size to distinguish
low-rate DDoS atacks from legitimate traﬃc. Te authors propose an expectation of packet
size measurement to distinguish atack traﬃc from legitimate traﬃc. Te proposed method
is independent of the atack patern; therefore, it can avoid the inherent shortcomings
of the signature-based metric. Moreover, this approach can achieve a large distance gap
between the atack traﬃcs and the legitimate traﬃcs, which could further contribute to a
low false-positive rate.
(10) Traﬃc Cluster Entropy: Reference [31] proposes traﬃc cluster entropy as detection metric
not only to detect DDoS atacks but also to distinguish DDoS atacks from Flash Events.
Te authors show that when ﬂash events are triggered, source address entropy increases
but the corresponding traﬃc cluster entropy does not increase. However, when DDoS
atack is launched, traﬃc cluster entropy also increases along with source address entropy.
(11) E–LDAT: Reference [5] proposes EﬁfLDAT, a lightweight extendedﬁfentropy metricﬁfbased
system for both DDoS ﬂooding atack detection and IP traceback. It aims to identify DDoS
atacks eﬀectively by measuring the metric diﬀerence between legitimate traﬃc and atack
traﬃc. IP traceback is performed using the metric values for an atack sample detected by
the detection scheme. Tis approach uses a generalized entropy metric with packet inten-
sity computation on the sampled network traﬃc with respect to time. Te authors show
that EﬁfLDAT works well for detecting four classes of DDoS ﬂooding atacks, including
constant rate, pulsing rate, increasing rate and subgroup atacks.
(12) Machine Learning: Reference [32] proposes machine learning to detect and mitigate known
and unknown DDoS atacks in real time environments. Te authors chose an Artiﬁcial
Neural Network (ANN) algorithm to detect DDoS atacks based on speciﬁc characteristic
features (paterns) that separate DDoS atack traﬃc from genuine traﬃc.
(13) Flow Correlation Coeﬃcient: Reference [42] proposes a discrimination algorithm using
ﬂow correlation coeﬃcient as a similarity metric among suspicious ﬂows. Te authors
present theoretical proofs for the feasibility of the proposed discrimination method.
(14) Multifractal Detrended Fluctuation Analysis(MF–DFA): Reference [36] proposes the al-
gorithm of multifractal detrended ﬂuctuation analysis to explore the change in terms of
multifractal characteristics over a small scale of network traﬃc due to low rate DDoS
atacks. Trough wavelet analysis, the singularity and bursty of network traﬃc under low
15


rate DDoS atacks are estimated by using Holder exponent. Te diﬀerence values, known
as D–value, of Holder exponent of network traﬃc between normal and under low rate
DDoS atack situations are calculated. Te D–value is used as the basis to determine low
rate DDoS atacks. A detection threshold is set based on the statistical results. Te presence
of low rate DDoS atacks can be conﬁrmed through comparing D–value with detection
threshold. Experiments on detection performance have been performed in the test-bed
network and simulation platform. Te extensive experimental results are congruent with
the theoretical analysis.
(15) FlowTrApp: Reference [7] proposes DDoS defense using FlowTrApp. Sofware Deﬁned
Network (SDN) provides a central control over the network which helps in geting the
global view of the network. FlowTrApp which performs DDoS detection and mitigation
using some bounds on two per ﬂow based traﬃc parameters that is ﬂow rate and ﬂow
duration of a ﬂow. It atempts to detect atack traﬃc ranging from low rate to high rate
and long lived to short lived atacks using an SDN engine consisting of sFlow based ﬂow
analytics engine sFlow-RT and an OpenFlow controller.
(16) K–Nearest Neighbors traﬃc classiﬁcation with correlation analysis (CKNN): Reference
[38] presents a detection approach based on K-nearest neighbors traﬃc classiﬁcation with
correlation analysis to detect DDoS atacks. Te approach exploits correlation information
of training data to improve the classiﬁcation accuracy and reduce the overhead caused
by the density of training data. Aiming at solving the huge cost, the authors also present
a grid-based method named r-polling method for reducing training data involved in the
calculation.
(17) Matching Pursuit and Orthogonal Matching Pursuit algorithms: Reference [2] proposes to
use Matching Pursuit and Orthogonal Matching Pursuit algorithms for DDoS detection.
Te major contribution of the paper is the proposition of 1D KSVD algorithm as well as its
tree based structure representation (clusters), that can be applied to detect low-rate DDoS
atacks and network anomalies. Te method maintains the features of malicious traﬃc in
form of tree to improve the classiﬁcation performance and to optimize the implementation
in terms of time complexity.
6
CONCLUSIONS
In this paper, we presented the classiﬁcation and literature review of DDoS atacks. In spite of
scrupulous research over the years to mitigate DDoS atacks, they still exist today, in fact, with
larger intensities and impacts as there are diﬀerent angles to consider. We also described some of
the commonly used defense mechanisms. Also, we presented a literature review of the defenses for
low-rate DDoS atacks that have not been handled eﬀectively till today.
